lessons.title: Modes of Transportation
lessons.body: In East Africa, getting around means knowing your matatu from your boda boda. A matatu is a minibus taxi, common in Kenya and Tanzania. In Uganda, they call them taxis. Fares depend on distance and time of day. For example, in Nairobi, a matatu from CBD to Westlands costs around 50-100 KSh. Boda bodas are motorcycle taxisâfast but risky. Always agree on the price before you hop on. In Tanzania, you'll find daladalas (minibuses) and bajajis (three-wheeled tuk-tuks). Bajajis are cheaper than taxis for short trips, often 2000-5000 TSh. For longer journeys, buses like Modern Coast or Tahmeed run between major cities. A bus from Nairobi to Mombasa takes about 8 hours and costs 1000-1500 KSh. Trains are limited but scenic: the TAZARA railway from Dar es Salaam to Zambia, or the new SGR from Nairobi to Mombasa. Boats are essential in places like Zanzibar or Lake Victoria. Always carry small billsâconductors rarely have change. Learn key phrases: 'Ningependa kwenda...' (I would like to go to...), 'Bei ni ngapi?' (How much is it?), 'Shusha hapa' (Stop here). Safety tip: avoid unlicensed taxis; use apps like Uber or Bolt in cities. In rural areas, pick-up trucks (malori) often carry passengers in the backâcheap but uncomfortable. Remember, 'safari' means journey, not just wildlife tour. So when someone says 'safari njema,' they wish you a good trip.

lessons.title: Buying Tickets and Making Reservations
lessons.body: Buying tickets in East Africa can be done at the station, online, or through a mobile app. For buses, companies like Easy Coach, Modern Coast, and Tahmeed have websites or agents. You can also use platforms like BuuPass or QuickBus in Kenya. A ticket from Nairobi to Kisumu costs about 1000-1500 KSh. For trains, the SGR (Standard Gauge Railway) requires booking online at metickets.crbc.co.tz or via the official app. A second-class ticket from Nairobi to Mombasa is around 1000 KSh. Always book in advance during holidaysâChristmas and Easter fill up fast. When you arrive at the station, you'll need to show ID (passport for foreigners, national ID for locals). For matatus, you don't reserve; you just pay the conductor. But for long-distance buses, you can reserve a seat by phone. Say: 'Nataka kukata tikiti' (I want to buy a ticket). 'Nina nafasi?' (Do you have space?). 'Naweza kulipa kwa M-Pesa?' (Can I pay with M-Pesa?). M-Pesa is a mobile money serviceâwidely accepted. For flights, use apps like Skyscanner or local airlines like Precision Air, Jambojet, or RwandAir. A one-way flight from Dar es Salaam to Zanzibar can be as low as $50 if booked early. Keep your ticket safeâsome conductors check multiple times. If you need to change your ticket, ask: 'Naweza kubadilisha tikiti?' (Can I change my ticket?). Refunds are rare, so confirm dates. For reservations at hotels or safaris, use Booking.com or local tour operators. Always get a written confirmation via SMS or email. Tip: buy tickets from official counters to avoid scams.

lessons.title: At the Airport/Bus Station
lessons.body: Navigating an airport or bus station in East Africa requires patience and Swahili. At the airport, you'll first go to check-in. Show your passport and ticket. The agent will ask: 'Una mizigo mingapi?' (How many bags?). You'll place bags on the scale. Excess baggage costs extraâoften $10-20 per kilo. Then you go through security. They may ask you to remove shoes, belts, and laptops. After security, find your gate. Listen for announcements: 'Ndege ya kwenda Nairobi inaondoka sasa' (The plane to Nairobi is departing now). At bus stations, it's more chaotic. In Nairobi's Machakos or Mombasa's Mwembe Tayari, touts will shout destinations. Ignore them and go to the official ticket office. Ask: 'Basi la kwenda Arusha linaondoka saa ngapi?' (What time does the bus to Arusha leave?). Times are often in Swahili: saa moja (7 AM), saa mbili (8 AM), etc. Swahili time starts at 6 AM, so 7 AM is saa moja. For buses, you'll load your luggage in the hold. Keep your ticketâa conductor may check it. On board, you'll be given a seat number. If someone sits in your seat, say: 'Samahani, hii ni kiti changu' (Excuse me, this is my seat). At airports, after landing, you'll go through immigration. Have your visa or entry permit ready. Customs may ask: 'Una kitu cha kutangaza?' (Do you have anything to declare?). Then you collect your bags from the carousel. If your bag is lost, go to the airline desk and say: 'Mizigo yangu haipo' (My luggage is missing). Always keep your valuables with you. At bus stations, watch out for pickpockets. Use a money belt. If you need help, ask a uniformed official: 'Naweza kupata msaada?' (Can I get help?).

lessons.title: Asking for and Giving Directions
lessons.body: Getting lost in a Swahili-speaking area is easy, but asking for directions is straightforward. Start with a polite greeting: 'Samahani' (Excuse me). Then ask: 'Njia ya kwenda... iko wapi?' (Where is the way to...?). For example, 'Njia ya kwenda sokoni iko wapi?' (Where is the way to the market?). People will often reply with landmarks: 'Panda mlima' (Go up the hill), 'Shuka' (Go down), 'Kulia' (Turn right), 'Kushoto' (Turn left), 'Moja kwa moja' (Straight ahead). Distances are given in time: 'Dakika tano kwa miguu' (Five minutes on foot). If you need to confirm, repeat: 'Kulia? Kushoto?' (Right? Left?). In rural areas, directions might refer to trees, churches, or shops: 'Baada ya kanisa, pinduka kushoto' (After the church, turn left). If someone gives directions too fast, say: 'Tafadhali, polepole' (Please, slowly). To give directions, use the imperative: 'Nenda' (Go), 'Geuka' (Turn), 'Vuka barabara' (Cross the road). If you're giving directions to a taxi driver, say: 'Nipeleke kwenye...' (Take me to...). For example, 'Nipeleke kwenye hoteli ya Serena' (Take me to Serena Hotel). If you're on a boda boda, you might say: 'Pita hapa' (Pass here), 'Simama hapa' (Stop here). If you're lost, look for a petrol station or a shopâpeople there are used to giving directions. Avoid asking strangers at night. In cities, use Google Maps offlineâdownload the map before you go. But remember, many small streets aren't labeled. So combine tech with asking. Key phrases: 'Nimepotea' (I am lost), 'Niko wapi?' (Where am I?), 'Mbali?' (Is it far?). If someone says 'karibu' (welcome), they might be inviting you to their homeâpolitely decline if you're not comfortable. Always thank them: 'Asante sana' (Thank you very much).

lessons.title: Talking About Travel Plans
lessons.body: Talking about travel plans in Swahili helps you share your itinerary and make arrangements. Start with the future tense: 'Nitakwenda' (I will go), 'Tutasafiri' (We will travel). For example, 'Kesho nitakwenda Arusha' (Tomorrow I will go to Arusha). To ask about someone's plans: 'Utakwenda wapi?' (Where will you go?). 'Utabaki siku ngapi?' (How many days will you stay?). If you're planning a trip, you might say: 'Nataka kufanya safari' (I want to take a trip). 'Nina mpango wa kwenda Zanzibar' (I have a plan to go to Zanzibar). To discuss dates: 'Wiki ijayo' (Next week), 'Mwezi ujao' (Next month), 'Mwaka huu' (This year). For example, 'Nitakwenda Mombasa wiki ijayo' (I will go to Mombasa next week). If you're traveling with others: 'Tutasafiri pamoja' (We will travel together). To ask about cost: 'Safari itagharimu kiasi gani?' (How much will the trip cost?). To book: 'Nahitaji kukata tikiti' (I need to buy a ticket). If you're unsure: 'Labda nitakwenda' (Maybe I will go). To express a wish: 'Ningependa kwenda' (I would like to go). Use 'kwa' for transport: 'kwa basi' (by bus), 'kwa ndege' (by plane), 'kwa treni' (by train). For example, 'Nitakwenda kwa basi' (I will go by bus). To ask about duration: 'Safari itachukua muda gani?' (How long will the trip take?). Answers: 'Saa mbili' (Two hours), 'Siku moja' (One day). If you're inviting someone: 'Unataka kuja na mimi?' (Do you want to come with me?). To confirm: 'Tutaonana kesho' (We will see each other tomorrow). If plans change: 'Nimebadilisha mipango' (I have changed plans). Practice these phrases with a friend. Write your own travel plan in Swahili: 'Mwezi ujao, nitakwenda Nairobi kwa ndege. Nitakaa siku tatu. Nitakwenda kwenye makumbusho ya Nairobi.' This builds confidence. Remember, 'safari' means journey, so 'safari njema' means 'good journey'.

lessons.title: Cultural Tips: Travel Etiquette
lessons.body: Traveling in East Africa requires respecting local customs. Greetings are essential. Always greet before asking for anything. Say 'Jambo' or 'Habari' (Hello/How are you?). In Tanzania, 'Shikamoo' is for elders (they reply 'Marahaba'). In Kenya, 'Sasa' is casual. When you enter a shop or office, greet everyone. It's rude to jump straight to business. Dress modestly, especially in Muslim areas like Zanzibar or coastal towns. Women should cover shoulders and knees. Men should avoid shorts in rural areas. When eating, use your right hand. If offered food, accept a little even if you're not hungryâit's polite. In restaurants, tipping is not mandatory but appreciated (10% in tourist areas). For transport, if you're in a matatu and an elderly person boards, offer your seat. On buses, don't put your feet on the seat. When taking photos, ask first: 'Naweza kupiga picha?' (Can I take a photo?). Some people, especially in Maasai communities, may expect payment. Bargaining is normal in markets, but not in shops with fixed prices. Start at half the asking price and negotiate with a smile. Don't lose your temper. If invited to someone's home, bring a small gift like fruit or sugar. Remove your shoes before entering. When leaving, say 'Asante kwa mwaliko' (Thank you for the invitation). In business settings, handshakes are common. Use both hands or your right hand. Don't use your left hand to give or receive. Public displays of affection are frowned upon. Also, avoid pointing with your fingerâuse your whole hand. If you're in a village, ask permission before entering a homestead. Respect elders: stand when they enter, and listen more than you speak. Finally, learn a few words in local languages like Kikuyu, Luo, or Maasaiâit shows respect. 'Asante' works everywhere. If you make a mistake, apologize: 'Samahani, sikujua' (Sorry, I didn't know). People are forgiving if you try.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Swahili for Travel & Transportation

This reference lesson consolidates the vocabulary, phrases, and cultural protocols you need to move people, goods, and yourself across East Africa. Whether you are a procurement officer flying into Dar es Salaam to inspect a coffee shipment, a sales lead taking the bus from Nairobi to Arusha for a distributor meeting, or an entrepreneur arranging boda-boda logistics in Kampala, the language of travel is the language of business. Swahili (Kiswahili) is the most widely spoken lingua franca in East Africa, with official status in Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and significant use in Rwanda, Burundi, and Mozambique. Mastering travel vocabulary gives you direct access to drivers, ticket agents, customs officials, and local partners without an intermediary.

1. Modes of Transportation â Njia za Usafiri

Table 1: Core transport vocabulary for business travel
Swahili English Business use
garivehicle / carGeneral term for road transport
basibusIntercity passenger travel
matatu / daladalaminibusUrban and peri-urban commuting
boda-bodamotorcycle taxiLast-mile delivery and rapid transit
trenitrainFreight and passenger rail
ndegeairplaneInternational and regional flights
mashuaboat / dhowLake and coastal transport
loritruckCargo and bulk goods
usafiri wa ummapublic transportGeneral commuting context
usafiri wa kibinafsiprivate transportCompany vehicles, charters

In business negotiations, always clarify the mode of transport before agreeing on delivery timelines. Tutasafiri kwa ndege (We will travel by plane) signals speed and higher cost; tutasafiri kwa lori (We will travel by truck) signals bulk capacity and longer lead times. Inland container depots in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam connect to the Standard Gauge Railway and the Central Corridor, so specifying treni versus lori has direct cost implications.

2. Buying Tickets and Making Reservations â Kununua Tiketi na Kuweka Nafasi

Table 2: Ticketing and reservation phrases with business applications
Swahili phrase English meaning When to use
Nataka tiketi ya kwendaâ¦I want a ticket toâ¦At ticket counters
Bei ya tiketi ni ngapi?How much is the ticket?Price negotiation
Ninaweza kuweka nafasi?Can I make a reservation?Advance booking
Tiketi ya kwenda na kurudiReturn ticketRound-trip planning
Nina mizigoI have luggage/cargoDeclaring goods
Naomba risitiPlease give me a receiptExpense accounting
Nafasi ya daraja la kwanzaFirst-class seatExecutive travel
Gari linaondoka saa ngapi?What time does the vehicle leave?Schedule confirmation

Always request a receipt (risiti) for business expenses. In Tanzania and Kenya, VAT-registered transport operators must issue fiscal receipts. For cargo, confirm whether the price includes ushuru (customs duty) and bima (insurance). If you are booking on behalf of a company, use tunahitaji (we need) rather than ninahitaji (I need) to signal institutional purchasing power.

3. At the Airport / Bus Station â Uwanja wa Ndege / Stesheni ya Basi

Key locations and phrases: uwanja wa ndege (airport), stesheni ya basi (bus station), lango (gate), pasipoti (passport), viza (visa), ukaguzi wa usalama (security check), kupanda (to board), kushuka (to alight). At Julius Nyerere International Airport or Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, officials may ask Unakwenda wapi? (Where are you going?) and Una kitu cha kutangaza? (Do you have anything to declare?). Respond clearly and keep documents accessible. For bus stations, arrive early; mabasi often depart when full rather than on a strict timetable, so confirm tutaondoka saa ngapi (what time will we leave) with the conductor.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Travel Security

Do not accept unsolicited help with luggage or documents at airports and bus stations. Keep your passport, tickets, and cash in a secure inside pocket. Avoid displaying large sums of money when paying for tickets. Only use licensed taxis or verified ride-hailing apps; unlicensed boda-boda operators may not carry passenger insurance. In case of emergency, the police number in Kenya is 999 or 112; in Tanzania it is 112. Report lost documents immediately to your embassy and the local police station.

4. Asking for and Giving Directions â Kuuliza na Kutoa Maelekezo

Essential directional vocabulary: kushoto (left), kulia (right), moja kwa moja (straight ahead), nyuma (behind), mbele (in front), karibu na (near), mbali na (far from), kona (corner), daraja (bridge), soko (market), benki (bank). To ask: Samahani, njia ya kwendaâ¦ iko wapi? (Excuse me, where is the way toâ¦?). To give: Pita moja kwa moja, kisha geuka kushoto kwenye taa za barabarani (Go straight, then turn left at the traffic lights). In business contexts, precise directions matter for logistics. When directing a driver to a warehouse, use landmarks: Baada ya daraja la pili, geuka kulia (After the second bridge, turn right). Confirm understanding with Umenielewa? (Did you understand me?) and expect Nimeelewa (I understood).

5. Talking About Travel Plans â Kuzungumza kuhusu Mipango ya Safari

Future tense in Swahili uses the prefix -ta-: Nitasafiri kesho (I will travel tomorrow), Tutafika Jumanne (We will arrive on Tuesday). For planned business trips: Tunapanga kukutana na mteja Arusha (We plan to meet a client in Arusha). Useful time markers: kesho (tomorrow), kesho kutwa (day after tomorrow), wiki ijayo (next week), mwezi ujao (next month). When confirming schedules, say Tutawasili saa tatu asubuhi (We will arrive at 9 a.m. â Swahili time counts from 6 a.m., so saa tatu asubuhi is 9 a.m.). Always clarify whether times are saa za Kiswahili (Swahili time) or saa za Kiingereza (English time) to avoid costly misunderstandings.

6. Cultural Tips: Travel Etiquette â Desturi za Safari

Greetings precede all business. Begin with Habari (How are you?), Shikamoo to elders (respectful greeting), and respond Marahaba. When boarding public transport, offer seats to elders and women with children. In shared taxis and matatus, greeting fellow passengers with Habari zenu is expected. Dress modestly for travel, especially in coastal and Muslim-majority areas like Mombasa and Zanzibar. When negotiating fares, remain calm and polite; aggression damages relationships. Tipping is appreciated but not always mandatory â for porters and drivers, 1,000â5,000 TZS or 100â500 KES is customary. Always ask permission before photographing people, vehicles, or premises. In business meetings, accept tea or water when offered; refusing can be read as rejection of hospitality.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Learn the difference between saa za Kiswahili and saa za Kiingereza before confirming any departure time.
  • Always request a risiti (receipt) for business travel and cargo expenses.
  • Confirm whether quoted prices include ushuru (customs) and bima (insurance).
  • Carry your pasipoti, viza, and ticket copies in a secure place.
  • Use tunahitaji (we need) when booking on behalf of your company to signal institutional authority.
  • Greet before transacting: Habari, Shikamoo, Marahaba.
  • Avoid unlicensed boda-boda and taxis; use verified operators.
  • Keep emergency numbers saved: 112 (Tanzania), 999/112 (Kenya), 112 (Uganda).

Further Reading

  • East African Community â Regional Integration & Transport
  • African Development Bank â Transport Sector
  • Kiswahili.net â Free Swahili Language Resources
  • United Republic of Tanzania â Official Government Portal
  • Tanzania Revenue Authority â Customs & Travel Information

quiz.q: What is a 'matatu'?
quiz.explanation: Matatu is a minibus taxi common in Kenya and Tanzania.

quiz.q: How do you say 'How much is it?' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: 'Bei ni ngapi?' means 'How much is it?'.

quiz.q: What is the Swahili word for 'bicycle'?
quiz.explanation: Baiskeli is borrowed from English and means bicycle.

quiz.q: In Swahili time, what does 'saa moja' mean?
quiz.explanation: Swahili time starts at 6 AM, so saa moja is 7 AM.

quiz.q: What is the common mobile money service in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: M-Pesa is Kenya's leading mobile money service.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'Where is the way to the market?' in Swahili?
options: A) Njia ya kwenda sokoni iko wapi?
quiz.explanation: This is the direct translation for asking directions to the market.

quiz.q: What does 'kushoto' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Kushoto' means left in Swahili.

quiz.q: What is the SGR train in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: SGR stands for Standard Gauge Railway, connecting Nairobi and Mombasa.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I would like to go to...' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: 'Ningependa kwenda' is a polite way to say 'I would like to go'.

quiz.q: What is a 'boda boda'?
quiz.explanation: Boda boda is a motorcycle taxi common in East Africa.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'Can I pay with M-Pesa?' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: This is the correct way to ask if you can pay with M-Pesa.

quiz.q: What does 'safari njema' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Safari njema' means 'good journey'.

quiz.q: At what time does Swahili time start?
quiz.explanation: Swahili time starts at 6 AM, so 7 AM is saa moja.

quiz.q: How do you say 'Turn right' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: 'Geuka kulia' means turn right.

quiz.q: What is a 'daladala'?
quiz.explanation: Daladala is the Swahili term for minibus in Tanzania.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I am lost' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: 'Nimepotea' means 'I am lost'.

quiz.q: What does 'karibu' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Karibu' means welcome.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'Where will you go?' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: 'Utakwenda wapi?' is the future tense for 'Where will you go?'.

quiz.q: What is the polite way to greet an elder in Tanzania?
quiz.explanation: 'Shikamoo' is a respectful greeting for elders in Tanzania.

quiz.q: How do you say 'Excuse me' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: 'Samahani' means 'Excuse me' or 'Sorry'.

quiz.q: What does 'kwa ndege' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Kwa ndege' means 'by plane'.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'How long will the trip take?' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: This is the correct way to ask about trip duration.

quiz.q: What is a 'bajaji'?
quiz.explanation: Bajaji is a three-wheeled tuk-tuk common in Tanzania.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I need to buy a ticket' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: 'Nahitaji kukata tikiti' means 'I need to buy a ticket'.

quiz.q: What does 'moja kwa moja' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Moja kwa moja' means 'straight ahead'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'Thank you very much' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: 'Asante sana' means 'Thank you very much'.

quiz.q: What is the Swahili word for 'airport'?
quiz.explanation: 'Uwanja wa ndege' means airport.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'Can I get help?' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: 'Naweza kupata msaada?' means 'Can I get help?'.

quiz.q: What does 'polepole' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Polepole' means slowly.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I have changed plans' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: 'Nimebadilisha mipango' means 'I have changed plans'.
